Biometric data should NEVER be used for security. Your point is valid, but there is a more fundamental reason why it shouldn't be used:

  1. You enter your fingerprint / face / etc. The reader doesn't store the fingerprint, it stores a hash value that represents your fingerprint . This hash value uniquely represents you.

  2. Your hash (and everyone else' hash) gets stolen off some database that wasn't configured correctly.

  3. Now your hash is forever known.

When this happens with a normal password, you just change your password.

But, you can't change your fingerprint, so you can't change your hash. So, one broken data base and your biometric data is exposed for life.

(I'm over simplifying things a bit. There are ways to layer the hash value with salting functions ... but someone who doesn't configure the database right probably won't get that right either...)

If some central authenticator of fingerprint data lost everyones' salted hashes, it wouldn't matter. If they weren't salting the hashes, well, that would be sad. You would have to use another finger, or they would upgrade their hardware to do the hash differently. Ostensibly there's quite a bit of processing that happens after you scan your finger print, and the "hash" could just be salted before it is sent.

Lots of good reasons to not use biometric data, loss of the hash meaning your biometrics were forever compromised is probably not among them.

For example, you can't expect it to run exactly how you want it to out of the box. I learned this from years of experience using Linux. Commercial OS usually has a certain amount of auto-configuration. This is not the case with Linux. Sometimes things will work great, but not always, and if there's a bad mismatch, your graphics and sound can suck, for example. If you actually have the time to sit down and figure it out yourself, by all means do so but be aware it can be a significant amount of effort to customize, something you needn't much bother with in Microsoft or Apple.
